verdicts.reasoning: Both teams found the same root (unknown treated as a value, numbers asserted instead of derived from one rubric) and the same fix shape: Optional inputs, three-valued investor constraints with a check-with-investor group, readiness as advice, counterfactual gaps, pipeline fixes. A is the better base. Its coverage plus 'not assessed' scoring is exactly the flag's resolution and gives founders a single honest number instead of a range. Its pipeline fix is more correct when checked against the code: backend/pyproject.toml declares requires-python >=3.10 and mypy python_version 3.10, where datetime.fromisoformat rejects 'Z', so B's reliance on 3.11 accepting 'Z' is unsafe; and since can_advance only allows closed_won from term_sheet/negotiation, a WON entry without history provably passed every open stage through term_sheet, which B's '{initial_contact, terminal}' undercounts. A's plan also splits subtasks more finely. B contributes three things A lacks: reuse of the shared app/core/tri.py (Tri/Verdict) and FounderFacts (app/core/facts.py, from_slots) contract that T04 and T24 also use, instead of A's separate FundingProfile type; value_by_stage as a real replacement for the removed weighted_value; and the interval monotonicity property test. B's interval readiness is a sound alternative, but ranges are harder for low-literacy founders and add a second score shape; it is not adopted.

final.chosen: A's single rubric table with three-valued inputs (per-dimension coverage, 'not assessed', overall over assessed weight), with inputs carried in B's shared FounderFacts funding fields and constraints in the shared core/tri.py; investor constraints three-valued with readiness demoted to advice and fit from varying terms only; counterfactual gap impacts from the same rubric; A's state-machine-correct pipeline fixes plus B's value_by_stage.
final.why_chosen: One rubric definition feeds score, coverage, gating advice, next questions and gap impact, so they cannot disagree; unknown is legal so the frontend needs no invented defaults; readiness ranks and advises while only investor-published criteria exclude. Reusing T04's Tri/Verdict and the FounderFacts contract means one unknown-aware mechanism across schemes, funding and opportunities, and the conversation's stage/team answers fill readiness without re-asking. Deterministic, standard library only, offline.

design.algorithm: Unanswered rows add to the dimension's total weight but earn nothing; dimension score = earned points on the existing scale; coverage = answered weight / total weight; coverage < 0.5 -> score None. overall = weighted mean over assessed dimensions with weights renormalised; assessed weight < 0.5 -> overall None, band 'not enough answers'. Investors: Kleene AND over constraints. Gap impact(a) = score(facts with a.sets).overall - score(facts with a's inputs at their non-achieved value).overall, computed with dimensions forced assessed so impact equals rubric points; zero-impact actions dropped; sort by impact/effort, ties by dimension weight.

verdicts.reasoning: Both teams chose the same core (nullable columns with email only in users, drop SoftDeleteMixin for hard delete with cascades, server-only verification with renamed tiers, AES-GCM TypeDecorator with key ids and an HMAC blind index), and both match the flag resolutions and founder.py:23-39. They differ in details. A is right that phone must not stay unique, even as a unique blind index: family members share one phone in rural Tamil Nadu and identity already lives in users.email; B's unique phone_bi would reject a second founder on a shared phone. A keeps startup GSTIN/CIN/DPIIT as plain unique columns (public registry identifiers; hard delete already frees them), which is simpler than B's encrypted values plus three unique blind indexes. A also adds a production boot check and a gitignored per-machine dev key file. B adds things A lacks and that sharpen correctness: per-field provenance (self_reported / format_checked / verified:method) so 'you told us' is stored, not just displayed; first_graduate nullable (unknown is not false, today it defaults to False at founder.py:39); an explicit erasure_audit model with an HMAC subject hash rather than an unspecified 'audit row'; and a migration guard that aborts if rows exist. The final takes A's lookup/uniqueness choices and key handling, and B's provenance, first_graduate, erasure_audit and row-count guard.

final.chosen: Nullable founder/startup columns with identity only in users; per-field provenance and server-only verification with honest tier names; hard delete with cascades and a PII-free erasure_audit row; AES-GCM TypeDecorator with a keyring separate from JWT signing and one non-unique HMAC blind index for phone.
final.why_chosen: Each part removes one way the schema fights the product: nullable columns let partial profiles sync and make minimisation the default; provenance plus server-only verification means nothing typed or ticked is called verified (D11, no invented data); hard delete with the existing cascades makes erasure real and frees identifiers (D12); randomised AES-GCM with its own keyring and a blind index protects sensitive columns while keeping the one lookup that matters, without forbidding shared family phones. One migration while no real data exists, using cryptography which is already installed, fully offline.

verdicts.reasoning: The two designs converge on the same artefact: a persisted plan snapshot with statuses, coverage-based confidence with a spoken range, three-valued applicability that lists conditional milestones, c_grant split into c_seed_grant (Validation) and c_growth_funding (Growth), and a remaining() function over the planner's existing critical-path code (both rightly reject NetworkX as a second graph implementation). A is the better base: it writes a plan row on every build behind a MemoryPlans/SqlPlans protocol, so the tracker always has a plan_id and the design works without PostgreSQL (offline constraint), whereas B keeps anonymous plans in the 6-hour session envelope until sign-in, leaving F-B2-022 unfixed for anonymous founders; A reuses T04's three-valued evaluate (a declared dependency) instead of a planner-local tri-state; A scopes statuses by plan and reconciles strictly on (id, template_hash), where B's fallback 'same id and title' could carry a status across packs that reuse a title; and A's tasks map more finely, including the localStorage import and the cohort band. B adds two things worth taking: plan staleness and supersede driven by T06's derivation key (plan_key = derive_key('roadmap', s)) rather than A's ad hoc idea_version + PLANNER_SLOTS, which is exactly the shared mechanism T31 depends on; and target_stages declared on funding templates in pack data so annotate.py places schemes by T01 Stage from reviewed data rather than a hard-coded stage list. B's property test on remaining() is also kept.

final.chosen: Persisted plan snapshot (MemoryPlans/SqlPlans) written on every build, keyed by T06's plan_key with statuses scoped to the plan and reconciled on (id, template_hash); coverage-based confidence with spoken ranges; T04 three-valued applicability listing conditional milestones; stage-specific funding milestones with target_stages in pack data; remaining() over the existing graph code.
final.why_chosen: Making the roadmap a stored, owned artefact fixes the root: with its own row and id, milestone ids need only be unique within a plan (keeping pack overrides), the tracker has something durable to point at, Ideate reads the same plan as Talk, and cohort progress can read statuses. T06's plan_key decides exactly when a plan is stale; T04's evaluator and T01's Stage are reused rather than duplicated. The other changes make the artefact honest (confidence from what is known, conditional milestones instead of silent drops, grants where they fund the work) and live (remaining critical path from statuses). Deterministic, offline, no new dependency.

verdicts.reasoning: Both teams agree on package-relative paths (config.py:14 and :115 really are CWD-relative), an OS-scheduler-only trigger with a lock and per-step ledger, an explicit ERASURE_MAP with an 'anon' guard and a metadata coverage test, and consent tombstones deleted a year after erasure. The real split is how erasure and retention reach in-process state. A runs the steps inside the app: scripts/nightly.py (started by the OS scheduler) calls a localhost, token-protected endpoint so every delete goes through the same delete_session path as the founder's DELETE route (store stack + board.forget), and runs the same runner standalone when the app is down (when there is no memory to clear). That is exactly F-B5-016's resolution and fits decision 0010, which says the app is one process. A also notes that CachedStore.delete already drops sess:{id}, so the leak only comes from deleting through the inner store. B runs out of process and bridges to memory with a new erased_sessions table and Redis tombstones that the T12 sweeper applies later. That adds a table, a migration and eventual consistency, and it cannot work on the memory store without a database. B's objection that an endpoint 'reaches one worker only' does not apply under 0010. A wins on the core. B adds small hardening worth keeping: steps report 'skipped: no database' instead of succeeding silently, erase_sessions refuses empty or over-1000-id batches and non-UUID owners, and step status appears in /health as well as the 5.4.3 page.

final.chosen: A's in-app maintenance service: OS scheduler starts scripts/nightly.py, which triggers the runner inside the app through a localhost token endpoint (standalone fallback when the app is down); Redis SET NX / O_EXCL file run lock; atomic per-step JSON ledger with catch-up; package-relative paths; explicit erasure map with sentinel guards and a shared delete_session; consent tombstones. Plus B's 'skipped: no database' reporting, batch/UUID guards and /health status.
final.why_chosen: Running every delete through the same in-app path as the founder's DELETE reaches database, Redis and the in-memory job board together without new tables or infrastructure (F-B5-016, decision 0010). The OS scheduler gives one run by construction (F-A5-028); the lock and ledger cover manual overlap, missed nights and failure streaks (F-B5-013). Package-relative paths remove CWD dependence for app, scripts and tests. Consent tombstones satisfy both written retention rules. Works offline, with memory stores and without Redis.

design.components: 1) core/paths.py: BACKEND_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]; resolve(p) returns absolute p unchanged, else BACKEND_DIR / p. Settings: env_file = BACKEND_DIR/'.env'; validators resolve research_cache_dir, a new state_dir ('.state') and the T30 key dir. 2) maintenance/runner.py: Step(name, fn); run(steps, trigger) takes the lock, runs each step in its own try/except with a timeout, writes the ledger, releases. A step that needs a database and has none records 'skipped: no database'. Steps: research_cache_purge (T08 purge), retention (sessions idle > 90 days and not saved per D4; anonymous plans with them; consent tombstones older than 1 year; logs older than 30 days), session_upgrade_all (T34), cohort_projection_rebuild (T34 / 5.5.5.2), warming (2.2.6) when it lands. 3) maintenance/lock.py: Redis SET maint:lock <run_id> NX EX 3h; else O_CREAT|O_EXCL lock file in state_dir with pid and start time, stale after 3h; a held lock records 'already running' and exits 0. 4) maintenance/ledger.py: state_dir/maintenance.json {step: {last_start, last_success, last_error, consecutive_failures}} written atomically (tmp + os.replace). Alert = consecutive_failures >= 2, exposed via GET /internal/maintenance/status for 5.4.3 and summarised in /health. 5) Trigger: POST /internal/maintenance/run (localhost check + MAINTENANCE_TOKEN; never takes a user id); scripts/nightly.py posts to it or, on connection refused, runs the runner standalone. App lifespan: if a daily step's last_success is older than 26h, schedule one background catch-up (lock prevents duplicates). Runbook: Windows Task Scheduler entry with 'run as soon as possible after a missed start', and a cron/anacron line. 6) services/erasure.py: ERASURE_MAP of every personal table and key path (users; founders via users.founder_id with startups/profile_completeness/documents cascading; agent_sessions.user_id; plans.user_id (T31); consents -> tombstone) plus non-DB targets via one shared delete_session(id) = get_store().delete + board.forget + result store delete, also used by the DELETE route and retention. erase_user(user_id) refuses None, '', 'anon', non-UUID values and ids not in users; erase_sessions refuses empty lists or more than 1000 ids; rows deleted in one transaction, then Redis/memory cleared, then erasure_log written. NOT_PERSONAL lists reference and derived tables. 7) Consent tombstones: on erasure each consent becomes {subject_ref = HMAC(blind_index_key, user_id), purpose, policy_version, given_at, withdrawn_at, erased_at} with no personal content; deleted 1 year after erased_at; plain retention keeps consents for the data's life plus one year. Recorded in SYSTEM-DESIGN 5.4 and decision 0011, flagged for the 3.2.6 legal review.

design.algorithm: Retention selects by last_active (works while user_id is 'anon') and deletes through delete_session. Erasure selects by owner and refuses until T17 links sessions to real users. verdicts.reasoning: Both teams name the same root: the replay boundary sits above the code under test, and the report is not deterministic. Both add an unscripted-question check, assertions on s.roadmap and a --check report mode. They differ on where to replay. A replays at the research.sources function layer (papers, paper_count, trials, projects, patents, epo_patents all take (client, query, cache)), which is exactly F-A5-003's resolution: scan() and novelty.check() post-processing run for real, fixtures stay readable JSON, nothing above HTTP stores credentials, and degraded variants are a per-source status override. B replays at the HTTP boundary keyed by T08's canonical_key. That would also cover parsing, but canonical_key and Entry do not exist yet in backend/app/research (they are T08 future work that T33 would block on). B also needs a research_client_factory hook in production scan/novelty, larger raw-body fixtures, and re-records on every query-building change, which the flag explicitly wanted to avoid. Parsing (_work, epo_documents) is better covered by small unit tests. On dynamic answers, A keys them by the question's recorded source ('dynamic:<source>', then 'dynamic'), which scales past one dynamic question. B has a single answers.dynamic. A's --check ignores only the Generated line, keeping the useful timestamp as the flag resolution says. A's tasks also map each flag through two concrete subtasks with meta-tests. B's idea of keeping the old 'scan'/'novelty' fixture fields for one PR, to diff old and new output, is a good rollout step and is noted in the final rollout.

final.chosen: Source-layer record/replay with degraded variants via pytest parametrisation, an unscripted-question check plus source-keyed dynamic answers, assertions on s.roadmap, and a --check mode for the report.
final.why_chosen: Replay at the source-function boundary is the lowest layer that is still stable and readable, so the logic the quality set claims to check actually runs, and the same recordings yield degraded variants by overriding source status, with no network and no dependency on T08's future cache key. The unscripted check turns silent skips into failures while source-keyed answers let the payer question be scripted. Asserting on s.roadmap tests what the founder saw. --check keeps the committed report verifiable without losing its timestamp.

verdicts.reasoning: The two designs are close to identical in structure: a FORMAT number, one pure decode with an upgrade chain, UndecodableSession mapped to 410 and skip-and-count in /programme, a newer-format guard returning 503, a format column with an idempotent upgrade-all, a vocabulary step that re-keys idea_version results, and split tables as a nightly projection with Pydantic payload contracts. Both reject the same alternatives for sound reasons. B's save guard is more correct. SqlStore.save adds WHERE format <= FORMAT, so it is atomic against a newer worker that wrote after this one loaded. A's in-memory loaded_format check only catches documents that were already newer at load time, so in a mixed deploy a newer write between load and save would still be overwritten (F-B2-002). B also makes the row columns (version, format) authoritative over copies inside the document, which matters because SqlStore.get merges row.version. B treats a Redis copy older than the row as a miss, and keeps one fixture document per historical format plus a --dry-run for the backfill. A adds a decode_error column so undecodable rows are marked and queryable, registers upgrade-all and the projection rebuild as T32 maintenance steps, and has a test forbidding ORM imports in the codec, which keeps steps pure. The final takes A's module, decode_error, maintenance registration and purity test, and B's SQL-level guard, row-authoritative decode, stale-copy rule, per-format fixtures and dry run. The decision record is numbered 0012 because T32 takes 0011.

final.chosen: Central session codec (FORMAT, pure upgrade chain, decode policy, newer-format guard enforced in SQL on save) + format and decode_error columns with an idempotent, dry-runnable upgrade-all registered as a maintenance step + vocabulary upgrade step through T01's mapping with result re-keying + split tables as a nightly projection with Pydantic payload contracts.
final.why_chosen: A single codec is the smallest thing that owns all five failure modes. It decides what an unreadable document means (410 or skip, never 500). It refuses formats newer than the code, atomically on save, so nothing is lost silently. It runs versioned upgrades including the vocabulary mapping. It stamps a format that a column exposes for backfill and as the split precondition. JSON stays the truth and the tables become a rebuildable projection, which keeps decision 0003 and the guarded write path. Pure Python, testable on the memory store, offline. It is also the registry other themes (T19 consents, T24 choice state, T01 renames) add their steps to.

design.components: 1) agents/session_codec.py (new; no ORM imports, enforced by a test): FORMAT = 2 (format 1 = today's unversioned docs); UPGRADES = {1: _v1_to_v2, ...} pure and idempotent dict->dict; decode(raw, *, row_version=None, row_format=None) -> Decoded{session, upgraded_from, idea_version_before}; encode(s) -> dict with 'format'. Row columns (version, format) are authoritative over copies inside the document. Errors SessionUnreadable(session_id, format, reason) and FormatTooNew(session_id, found, known). from_dict/to_dict become private helpers used only by the codec; enum restore is strict (an unknown value after upgrading is cleared to confidence 0 so it is asked again, never kept as a bare str). 2) Memory, Sql and Cached stores call decode/encode only. get() catches SessionUnreadable, logs agent_store.unreadable (ids, format, exception type, never document text) and the router maps it to 410 'This conversation cannot be resumed'; FormatTooNew -> 503 'saved by a newer version; try again shortly'. CachedStore treats a Redis copy that fails to decode, or is older than the row, as a miss and drops it. 3) Save guard: SqlStore.save writes format=FORMAT with WHERE format <= FORMAT (and the existing version check); MemoryStore compares the stored document's format; a refusal raises FormatTooNew. Until the column exists the guard checks the format inside the stored document. 4) store.get_many(ids) -> (sessions, unreadable_count); /programme returns sessions_unreadable. 5) Vocabulary step: maps slot enum values through T01's frozen old->new mapping (data); the same step moves idea_version to canonical codes; decode reports idea_version before/after and the store calls ResultStore.rekey(session_id, old, new) once so finished scan/council results survive. 6) Migration <n>_session_format: agent_sessions.format SMALLINT (add nullable + index, backfill via script, then NOT NULL default 1) and decode_error TEXT NULL. 7) scripts/upgrade_sessions.py (also a T32 maintenance step): batches WHERE format < FORMAT; decode -> encode -> version-checked UPDATE (skip/retry on conflict); undecodable rows counted and marked in decode_error; --dry-run; report of counts per source format; idempotent; prints remaining count. 5.5.5.1 precondition: count(format < FORMAT) == 0. 8) Projection (5.5.5.2): analytics tables rebuilt nightly by T32's runner from decoded JSON at the current format; nested payloads validated by Pydantic contracts (RoadmapContract from T31, CouncilContract from T35, NoveltyContract); invalid payloads skipped and counted; decision 0012 states JSON is the truth.
design.data_model: Document gains 'format'. agent_sessions gains format SMALLINT NOT NULL (indexed) and decode_error TEXT NULL. ResultStore gains rekey(session_id, old_iv, new_iv). Projection tables are derived and droppable. tests/fixtures/sessions/ holds one document per historical format.
design.algorithm: fmt = row_format or raw.get('format', 1); fmt > FORMAT -> FormatTooNew; while fmt < FORMAT: raw = UPGRADES[fmt](deepcopy(raw)); fmt += 1; build AgentSession, mapping KeyError/ValueError/TypeError/ValidationError to SessionUnreadable. Save: UPDATE ... WHERE id=:id AND version=:v AND format <= :FORMAT; zero rows with a newer stored format -> FormatTooNew. Backfill idempotent because decoding a current document is the identity and saves are version-checked.
files: backend/app/agents/ideation.py (to_dict/from_dict private, strict enum restore, idea_version on canonical codes)
design.rollout: 1) Codec with FORMAT=2 (step 1->2 only adds the key), decode policy and guard, all stores using it. 2) Format/decode_error columns (nullable), dry run, script backfill, then constraint; register upgrade-all as a nightly step. 3) Vocabulary step (FORMAT 3) when T01's mapping and T06's idea_version definition land. 4) Each later format change lands as a step, a fixture and a test in one PR; deploys roll forward only. 5) Before 5.5.5, run until COUNT(format < FORMAT) = 0, then build the projection with contracts.
design.offline: Codec and upgrades are pure Python and run on MemoryStore and in tests; the columns and script apply only where PostgreSQL exists.

verdicts.reasoning: Both teams agree on a criterion on every claim validated in code, a three-state founder-skill rule (unknown gives no bump, word-boundary match so 'python developer' counts as technical), and one structured panel call with per-seat validation, rule fallback for missing seats and breaker recording. A gets F-A1-020 right and B does not. A criterion alone does not fix the probe, because the rules.customer claim 'the closest domain names its usual buyers' really is about need but is neutral, so B's 'take the claim whose criterion matches from the low seat' would still read it out as the weakest point. A adds a direction (for/against/neutral) and quotes only 'against' claims as weaknesses and 'for' claims as strengths. A also keeps the design self-contained on its declared dependencies (T01, T13), while B routes the call through T15's egress gate, which T35 does not depend on. B contributes useful extras: ask_founder becomes a typed Question {criterion, text, duplicates_slot}, so T05 can bind the panel question and skip it when the slot is already filled; a PANEL_MODE=single|per_seat switch for one release to compare bands on the eval set before per-seat calls are removed; the skill vocabulary (with known non-technical entries) placed in T01's vocabulary module and matched by T10's word-boundary lexicon rather than a local list; a capped claim count with a prompt-only fallback when Gemini responseSchema is unavailable; and a T34 upgrader for the stored council shape. The final takes A's contract and B's extras, and uses T15's gate only if it exists.

final.chosen: Typed claim contract (criterion + direction) and typed panel question (criterion + duplicates_slot) validated in code; three-state founder-skill rule on the shared vocabulary; one batched panel call with per-seat validation, rule fallback, breaker recording, and a one-release PANEL_MODE comparison.
final.why_chosen: Criterion and direction on each claim make synthesis pairing a code decision (decision 0002), produced identically by rules and model seats, and they are the only option that stops neutral claims from being quoted as weaknesses. The skill rule claims only what is known. Batching cuts free-tier use sevenfold with no information loss because every seat already sees the same pack, and breaker recording ends quota stalls. A tagged question lets T05 route the founder's answer back to the right criterion. Rules remain the offline baseline.
